slides.title: Login, cart, checkout form. *Where does a website keep them?*
slides.sub: Pick the wrong one and a half-filled form disappears when the tab closes.

slides.title: HTTP doesn't *remember* you
slides.body: Logging in and clicking My Orders are two separate requests. So the browser has to remind the server it's still you.

slides.title: A cookie works like a cloakroom ticket
slides.body: The staff don't remember your face, they use your ticket number. Your browser shows its cookie on every request to that site the same way.

slides.title: Cookies are *tiny*
slides.of: per cookie, and it goes with every request to that site
slides.body: Browsers must allow at least 4,096 bytes per cookie. Source: RFC 6265, section 6.1.

slides.title: Your login cookie usually holds just *an ID*
slides.body: The server keeps the real details about you and uses that ID to look them up, the same way the cloakroom uses the number to find your coat.

slides.title: localStorage is why your cart is *still there tomorrow*
slides.body: localStorage stays until your code removes it or you clear your browser data. Closing the tab, or the whole browser, doesn't clear it.

slides.title: localStorage holds *a lot more than a cookie*
slides.body: It varies by browser. localStorage only stores strings, and it never goes to the server unless your code sends it. Source: MDN, Storage quotas.

slides.title: sessionStorage belongs to one tab
slides.body: That's why a half-filled checkout form can disappear when you close the tab. A second tab you open yourself gets its own sessionStorage.

slides.title: Every script on your page can read localStorage
slides.body: Analytics scripts and chat widgets too, so it's not a place for anything secret. Cookies can be read as well, unless the server marks them HttpOnly.

slides.title: Which one to use
slides.body: sessionStorage is for things that only matter in this tab. localStorage is for things you still want tomorrow.
